sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve on axes labeled z and x. It stays on the horizontal axis beside the origin, then rises in a straight slope.
sections.body_md:
The lasso objective is a squared residual plus an absolute penalty, with no leading one half on the square. The absolute value is not differentiable at zero, so stationarity uses a subdifferential. The subdifferential of \(\lvert t\rvert\) is the sign of \(t\) when \(t\neq 0\), and the whole interval \([-1,\ 1]\) at \(t=0\).

The gradient of \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert^2\) is \(2A^T(Ax-b)\). Stationarity says
\[
0\in 2A^T(Ax-b)+\lambda\,\partial\lVert x\rVert_1.
\]
When the columns of \(A\) are orthonormal, \(A^T A=I\) and \(z=A^T b\) turn this into a separate scalar condition on each coordinate. The solution is the soft-threshold map at level \(\lambda/2\):
\[
x_i=\mathrm{sign}(z_i)\max(\lvert z_i\rvert-\lambda/2,\ 0).
\]
The factor 2 in the residual gradient is why the threshold is \(\lambda/2\) and not \(\lambda\). The flat middle of the map is the set of inputs that land on zero.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For one coordinate with center \(z\) and weight \(\lambda>0\), the scalar objective is \((x-z)^2+\lambda\lvert x\rvert\). If \(z>\lambda/2\), then \(x=z-\lambda/2\). If \(z<-\lambda/2\), then \(x=z+\lambda/2\). If \(\lvert z\rvert\le\lambda/2\), then \(x=0\), and the subdifferential element \(s=2z/\lambda\) lies in \([-1,\ 1]\).

Without orthonormal columns the inclusion \(0\in 2A^T(Ax-b)+\lambda\,\partial\lVert x\rVert_1\) is still the stationarity condition. It no longer separates into a soft threshold of \(A^T b\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(A=I\), \(b=(9,\ -1)\), and \(\lambda=4\). Then \(z=b\) and the threshold is 2. The first input 9 is larger than 2, so the first coordinate is \(9-2=7\). The second input \(-1\) lies in \([-2,\ 2]\), so the second coordinate is 0. The kept coordinate equals 7, and the other coordinate is wiped out.

Subtracting the full weight 4 from 9 would give 5, which is the threshold for an objective that puts a one half in front of the square. This objective has no such one half. The second coordinate is zero because its input lost to the threshold, not because the penalty deleted every small coordinate by a different rule.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.body_md:
Do not use the threshold \(\lambda\) unless the square carries a leading one half. The gradient of the square, not a convention about the penalty, produces the 2.

The endpoint \(\lvert z\rvert=\lambda/2\) maps to zero. It is not a tiny nonzero value. The subdifferential at zero is the whole interval, so every input inside the threshold is explained by some slope in \([-1,\ 1]\).

Orthonormality is a hypothesis, not a minor simplification you can ignore. A non-orthogonal column couples the coordinates through \(A^T A\). The stationarity inclusion survives. The closed form does not.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: When the columns are not orthonormal, freeze every coordinate but one. The scalar piece that remains is still an absolute penalty plus a square in that coordinate, and its minimizer is a soft threshold of a center that depends on the frozen coordinates. One sweep of those exact minimizations is coordinate descent. The map derived here is the update that sweep uses. The sweep itself is the next skill.
